screens.title: UI Testing with Espresso
screens.subtitle: Simulate real user interactions on device to verify your app’s visible behavior and navigation.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why instrumented UI testing matters and how Espresso helps you write small, readable tests that run on a device or emulator. UI tests exercise the Android framework and your app’s screens, ensuring buttons, text fields, lists, and navigation work together when a real user interacts with them. You will see how Espresso synchronizes with the UI thread to reduce timing flakiness, which is a common source of intermittent failures. We’ll cover the minimal Gradle dependencies to enable instrumented tests, how to launch an activity safely with ActivityScenarioRule, and concrete Espresso patterns like onView, withId, typeText, closeSoftKeyboard, click, and matches. You’ll also follow an example test that adds a task and validates that it appears in a RecyclerView, plus a short walkthrough of list interactions and navigation to a detail screen. By the end, you’ll understand what to test in the UI, how Espresso avoids many timing issues, and the common missteps that cause unreliable tests. Think about a recent bug you saw in the UI — would a simple Espresso test have caught it early?

keyIdea.title: Why UI tests?
keyIdea.text: Instrumented UI tests run on device/emulator and confirm that views, input, and navigation work together under realistic conditions.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › UI Testing with Espresso

UI Testing with Espresso

Simulate user interactions on a device or emulator to verify UI behavior, input handling, and navigation flows.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

Why instrumented UI tests complement unit tests, how Espresso synchronizes with the UI thread, and a practical test that adds a task to a list.

Core focus

Reliable view matching, RecyclerView interactions, and common troubleshooting patterns like closing the soft keyboard and using idling resources.

Outcome

Write and run concise Espresso tests that validate UI flows and reduce regressions in visible behavior.

Common pitfall

Tests that fail from timing or keyboard issues rather than real bugs. We’ll cover how to avoid those failures.

Explore Key Topics
Why UI tests
Prevent regressions in real user flows.
Espresso basics
onView, matchers, actions, and assertions.
RecyclerView
Use espresso-contrib and RecyclerViewActions for list items.
Visual Concept
Device
Emulator or phone runs the instrumented tests and hosts the Android framework.
Espresso
Synchronizes actions with the UI thread and provides matchers and actions.
ActivityScenarioRule
Launches and manages the lifecycle of the activity under test.
RecyclerViewActions
Helpers to interact with list items during tests.
Quick start

Add the androidTestImplementation dependencies, place tests under src/androidTest, use ActivityScenarioRule to launch your screen, and write concise assertions with matches(isDisplayed()).

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why UI testing is distinct from unit testing, set up an instrumented test environment using Espresso and JUnit, and write basic tests that interact with views. You will learn how to launch activities reliably with ActivityScenarioRule, use onView with matchers to locate views, and perform actions like typing text, dismissing the soft keyboard, and clicking buttons. You will also practice validating results with assertions and verifying list interactions using RecyclerViewActions. These skills matter because UI tests catch problems that unit tests cannot — for example, a button that is visible in layout but blocked by the soft keyboard when the user types. One concrete example: after adding dependencies and creating a test that types a task title and clicks add, you will assert that the task text appears in the RecyclerView. A common misconception is that Espresso requires complex setup for every test; in reality, with a small set of dependencies and ActivityScenarioRule you can start validating key user flows quickly and reliably. This screen lists the objectives you will practice.

keyIdea.text: Set up Espresso tests, run instrumented tests on a device/emulator, and validate UI interactions in RecyclerView and navigation.

screens.title: What is UI Testing and Why it Matters
screens.subtitle: Instrumented UI tests validate the app's visible behavior on a device or emulator.

narration.text: UI testing, in this chapter's context, means instrumented testing that runs on an Android device or emulator and interacts with the Android framework. Unlike local unit tests that run on your development machine and verify business logic in isolation, instrumented UI tests exercise actual views, input methods, and navigation paths. This matters because many bugs only appear when views are rendered together, when the soft keyboard changes layout, or when a RecyclerView renders items dynamically. A concrete example is a task list screen: a unit test can verify the logic that creates a task, but only an instrumented UI test can confirm that typing a title into an EditText, dismissing the keyboard, pressing an Add button, and seeing the new item in the RecyclerView all work together. A common misconception is that UI tests are always slow and brittle. Espresso, however, is designed to be concise and reliable by synchronizing with the UI thread. That reduces timing-based flakiness compared to ad-hoc waits. Key takeaway: use unit tests for business logic, use instrumented Espresso tests to verify visible user flows and interactions that depend on the Android UI framework.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Instrumented UI tests run on device/emulator and verify that visible components interact correctly under real conditions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is UI Testing
Core Concept

What is UI Testing and Why it Matters

Instrumented tests run on device and validate visible behavior that unit tests cannot reproduce.

Definition
Tests that interact with the Android UI framework on a device or emulator to simulate real user interactions.
Concrete example
Typing a task title, tapping Add, and verifying the text appears in a RecyclerView on screen.
Misconception
They are not always flaky; Espresso’s synchronization reduces many timing failures when used properly.
Key Takeaway

Use instrumented UI tests to validate user-visible flows that depend on Android framework rendering and input behaviour.

Analogy

Think of unit tests as checking each appliance in a smart home individually, and instrumented UI tests as walking through the house to make sure the lights, doors, and thermostat interact correctly when you follow a real routine.

Why this matters
  • Find regressions that only surface when views compose and input methods change layout.
  • Validate navigation and list rendering end-to-end.
  • Complement unit tests to raise overall confidence in releases.

screens.title: Unit Tests vs Instrumented UI Tests
screens.subtitle: When to choose a local unit test and when to write an Espresso test.

narration.text: Understanding the difference between local unit tests and instrumented UI tests helps you choose the right test for each problem. Local unit tests run on the JVM and are excellent for verifying business logic in isolation — for example, verifying that a repository transforms data correctly or that a viewmodel computes a correct value. They are fast and inexpensive to run. Instrumented UI tests, by contrast, run on an Android device or emulator and interact with the Android UI framework; they validate that views render correctly, respond to user input, and navigate as intended. A concrete scenario: when you want to ensure a button press triggers navigation to a detail screen and that the correct data is shown, a unit test cannot verify the actual rendered view or the navigation stack. An Espresso test using ActivityScenarioRule and onView with matchers is required. A common misconception is to try to test UI rendering with only unit tests — that will miss layout, keyboard, and framework-dependent issues. Use both: unit tests for logic, Espresso tests for end-to-end visible behavior. This strategy keeps your test suite fast overall while catching UI regressions that only appear on a real screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose wisely
keyIdea.text: Unit tests validate logic quickly; instrumented tests validate UI behavior on device when the Android framework is involved.

Comparison

Misconception

screens.title: How Espresso Synchronizes with the UI Thread
screens.subtitle: Why Espresso reduces timing flakiness and when to use IdlingResource.

narration.text: Espresso reduces flakiness by synchronizing test actions with the Android UI thread and common background tasks. It waits for the UI thread to be idle and for default AsyncTasks and certain framework events to complete before performing the next action. This automatic synchronization handles many timing problems, but not every background operation. For long-running or custom background work, you need IdlingResource to tell Espresso when the app is idle. A concrete example: after clicking an Add button that triggers background database insertion, Espresso may proceed only if the insertion is performed on a scheduler that Espresso knows about. If not, the test can try to check the list before the new item appears. Registering an IdlingResource around the database operation or using test-specific synchronous operations fixes this. A common misconception is to wrap everything in arbitrary sleeps; sleeps create brittle timing and slow tests. Prefer Espresso synchronization and IdlingResource when needed. The takeaway: rely on Espresso’s built-in sync for most UI work, and add IdlingResource only for custom async operations that otherwise cause flakiness. How Espresso Synchronizes with the UI Thread means espresso waits for the ui thread to be idle; register idlingresource for custom background work to avoid flakiness.. In practical terms, why espresso reduces timing flakiness and when to use idlingresource.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Synchronization
keyIdea.text: Espresso waits for the UI thread to be idle; register IdlingResource for custom background work to avoid flakiness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Espresso Sync
Process Flow

How Espresso Synchronizes

Espresso waits for the UI thread and common framework tasks to finish before each action to reduce timing-related failures.

1
Detect UI idle
Espresso checks that the UI thread is not executing pending tasks before proceeding.
2
Handle known async work
Built-in synchronization covers common framework async patterns.
3
Register IdlingResource
For custom background threads or executors, register an IdlingResource so Espresso knows when to wait.
Example

If a button click triggers a background save, the test should wait for the save to complete. If Espresso does not know when the save is done, register an IdlingResource around the save operation or use a test-friendly synchronous path.

Common mistake

Using Thread.sleep() to wait for UI changes. This creates slow and flaky tests. Prefer synchronization and IdlingResource.

narration.text: Before you can write instrumented UI tests you must add the correct testing dependencies to your app module. The chapter shows a concise set of androidTestImplementation dependencies that include the AndroidX JUnit extension, Espresso core, espresso-contrib for RecyclerView actions, the Android test runner and rules, optional Mockito Kotlin for mocks, and navigation testing helpers when you need to assert navigation. After adding these dependencies and syncing Gradle, tests go under src/androidTest/java or kotlin. A common mistake is adding these dependencies to the wrong configuration or forgetting espresso-contrib when testing RecyclerView interactions. Once dependencies are in place, ActivityScenarioRule and onView calls become available and you can run tests on an emulator. This step is the practical foundation you need before writing the add-task test and list interactions. In practical terms, what to place under androidtestimplementation in app/build.gradle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Add Dependencies
Definition

Add Espresso Dependencies

Add androidTestImplementation dependencies to enable instrumented testing and RecyclerView actions.

dependencies {
    // ... other dependencies

    // Instrumented UI Testing with Espresso
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.test.ext:junit:1.1.5'
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.test.espresso:espresso-core:3.5.1'
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.test.espresso:espresso-contrib:3.5.1'
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.test:runner:1.5.2'
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.test:rules:1.5.0'
    androidTestImplementation 'org.mockito.kotlin:mockito-kotlin:3.2.0'
    androidTestImplementation 'androidx.navigation:navigation-testing:2.7.7'
}

After syncing, create tests under src/androidTest. Remember that espresso-contrib is needed for RecyclerViewActions and navigation-testing helps when asserting navigation components.

Pro tip

Keep test-only dependencies in androidTestImplementation so they don’t inflate release APKs.

Checklist
  • Add dependencies and sync Gradle.
  • Create src/androidTest/java or kotlin structure.
  • Use ActivityScenarioRule to launch activities in tests.
Common mistake

Forgetting espresso-contrib when testing RecyclerView leads to missing RecyclerViewActions support at runtime.

screens.title: Writing the addTask_displaysInList Test
screens.subtitle: A full Espresso test that types text, clicks add, and verifies the item appears.

narration.text: Let's walk through the addTask_displaysInList test shown in the chapter. This test launches TaskListActivity using ActivityScenarioRule, then performs a sequence: type the task title into the title EditText, type the description, close the soft keyboard, click the Add Task button, and finally assert that both title and description are displayed in the view hierarchy. The important Espresso idioms are onView to locate a view, withId or withText as matchers, perform to run actions like typeText and click, and check with matches(isDisplayed()) to assert visibility. Notice the use of closeSoftKeyboard after typing; this avoids the keyboard covering the Add button. A common error is omitting the closeSoftKeyboard call, which can make the Add click fail. The code also shows how you can check for text in the entire hierarchy with onView(withText(taskTitle)). check(matches(isDisplayed())). That is a simple, robust verification when the text uniquely identifies the item. Practice writing this test as is, and then try adding more specific matchers if your UI has multiple views with the same text. Writing the addTask_displaysInList Test means find the view, perform actions, close the keyboard when needed, then assert the expected view state.. In practical terms, a full espresso test that types text, clicks add, and verifies the item appears.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Find the view, perform actions, close the keyboard when needed, then assert the expected view state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › addTask Test
Code Walkthrough
// src/androidTest/java/com/cohortia/taskapp/ui/tasklist/TaskListActivityTest.kt
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class TaskListActivityTest {

    @get:Rule
    val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(TaskListActivity::class.java)

    @Test
    fun addTask_displaysInList() {
        val taskTitle = "Buy Groceries"
        val taskDescription = "Milk, Eggs, Bread"

        onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_title))
            .perform(typeText(taskTitle), closeSoftKeyboard())

        onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_description))
            .perform(typeText(taskDescription), closeSoftKeyboard())

        onView(withId(R.id.button_add_task))
            .perform(click())

        onView(withText(taskTitle))
            .check(matches(isDisplayed()))

        onView(withText(taskDescription))
            .check(matches(isDisplayed()))
    }
}
Concrete example
Typing and clicking Add should result in the new task text being visible on screen.
Common mistake
Omitting closeSoftKeyboard causes the keyboard to cover the Add button and may make the click fail.
Explanation
  • ActivityScenarioRule launches the activity and handles lifecycle in tests.
  • onView(withId(...)) finds a view by resource id; withText finds by visible text.
  • perform runs actions such as typeText and click; closeSoftKeyboard hides the keyboard.
  • check with matches(assertion) verifies view state like isDisplayed().
Key Takeaway

Follow the find-act-assert pattern and handle the soft keyboard to avoid false negatives in UI tests.

screens.title: Toggle and Delete Tests: Handling Item Actions
screens.subtitle: Tests that toggle completion and remove items from the list.

narration.text: The chapter includes tests that toggle a task's completion and delete tasks. The toggle test first adds a task using the same add pattern, then performs a click on the task title to toggle its state. Verifying the visual change can require custom matchers because default matchers cannot check properties like strikethrough or text color. The delete test example sketches a longClick or swipe-to-delete flow: it adds a task, then performs a longClick on the item and finally asserts that the task no longer appears. Important practical guidance here is to ensure your UI exposes accessible identifiers for delete controls or to provide a test-friendly delete action, because simple clicks may not be sufficient. For absence checks use doesNotExist() which is more reliable than not(isDisplayed()). A common pitfall is assuming isDisplayed false means the view was removed; it might still exist but be hidden. Use doesNotExist() to confirm removal. When verifying appearance or disappearance, choose matchers that reflect the actual UI changes your app makes, and prefer testable interactions like dedicated delete buttons or test-only hooks when possible. Toggle and Delete Tests: Handling Item Actions means use specific actions (longclick, swipe, or delete button) and verify absence with doesnotexist() for deletions.. In practical terms, tests that toggle completion and remove items from the list.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use specific actions (longClick, swipe, or delete button) and verify absence with doesNotExist() for deletions.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Toggle & Delete
Code Walkthrough
@Test
fun toggleTaskCompletion_updatesUI() {
    val taskTitle = "Clean Room"
    val taskDescription = "Vacuum and dust"

    // Add a task
    onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_title))
        .perform(typeText(taskTitle), closeSoftKeyboard())
    onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_description))
        .perform(typeText(taskDescription), closeSoftKeyboard())
    onView(withId(R.id.button_add_task)).perform(click())

    // Toggle completion by clicking the item
    onView(withText(taskTitle)).perform(click())

    // Verification may require a custom matcher; here we check it is still displayed
    onView(withText(taskTitle)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))
}

@Test
fun deleteTask_removesFromList() {
    val taskTitle = "Task to Delete"

    // Add task and then perform long click to delete
    onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_title)).perform(typeText(taskTitle), closeSoftKeyboard())
    onView(withId(R.id.button_add_task)).perform(click())

    onView(withText(taskTitle)).perform(longClick())

    // Verify the task no longer exists
    onView(withText(taskTitle)).check(doesNotExist())
}
Testing tip

Prefer explicit delete controls or test-only hooks so tests can trigger removal reliably without complex gestures.

Explanation
  • Use longClick or a delete button to trigger removal in tests.
  • Check absence with doesNotExist() to confirm the view was removed from the hierarchy.
  • Custom visual checks may need custom matchers for color or strikethrough.
Common pitfall

Using not(isDisplayed()) can pass even when the view still exists but is hidden; use doesNotExist() for removal assertions.

screens.title: Testing RecyclerView Interactions
screens.subtitle: Use espresso-contrib and RecyclerViewActions to click items at positions.

narration.text: RecyclerView is a common target for UI tests, and the chapter explains how to interact with items using RecyclerViewActions from espresso-contrib. First, ensure espresso-contrib is in your androidTestImplementation dependencies. Then add items to the list so the RecyclerView has content. Use onView(withId(R. id. recyclerView_tasks)) combined with RecyclerViewActions. actionOnItemAtPosition to perform a click on an item at a specific index. The example shows performing a click on position zero and then verifying the detail screen displays the expected title. If you need to interact with a specific item by content, use actionOnItem with a matcher like hasDescendant(withText("Task 1")). Remember that RecyclerView is optimized: not all items are in the view hierarchy at once, so actions target the adapter position rather than visible child indexes. A common error is assuming the same index across different data setups. For robust tests, add known test data first or find the item by text and use actionOnItem. This approach makes list interactions reliable and expressive in Espresso tests. Testing RecyclerView Interactions means use actiononitematposition or actiononitem with a matcher to interact with recyclerview items in tests.. In practical terms, use espresso-contrib and recyclerviewactions to click items at positions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RecyclerViewActions
keyIdea.text: Use actionOnItemAtPosition or actionOnItem with a matcher to interact with RecyclerView items in tests.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › RecyclerView Testing
Process

Testing RecyclerView Interactions

Use espresso-contrib's RecyclerViewActions to click items by position or by matching content.

onView(withId(R.id.recyclerView_tasks))
    .perform(RecyclerViewActions.actionOnItemAtPosition< TaskAdapter.TaskViewHolder >(0, click()))

// or
onView(withId(R.id.recyclerView_tasks))
    .perform(RecyclerViewActions.actionOnItem< TaskAdapter.TaskViewHolder >(hasDescendant(withText("Task 1")), click()))
Note
Remember to add test data so the RecyclerView contains predictable items for the position-based action.
Explanation
  • actionOnItemAtPosition targets a specific adapter position.
  • actionOnItem with a matcher targets a specific item by content, which is more robust across data changes.
  • Ensure espresso-contrib is included to access RecyclerViewActions.
Common pitfall

Assuming adapter positions are stable across runs. Prefer content matchers when possible.

screens.title: TaskDetailFragmentTest Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A guided test: add a task, navigate to detail, edit, save, and verify.

narration.text: The chapter's hands-on activity guides you through writing TaskDetailFragmentTest. The flow is practical: start TaskListActivity with ActivityScenarioRule, add a task so the list contains the item you will test, click the list item using RecyclerViewActions to navigate to TaskDetailFragment, verify the detail EditTexts show the correct title and description, modify the description, click Save, press back, and confirm the list shows the updated description. This test demonstrates interaction with both list navigation and fragment UI updates. A key concrete example in the starter code shows how to select the list item by its title using actionOnItem with hasDescendant(withText(originalTitle)) and then assert that the detail fields contain the expected text. One common source of flakiness in such tests is relying on implicit navigation timing: ensure the navigation component is ready by using appropriate matchers and consider navigation-testing helpers if needed. The practice reinforces the find-act-assert pattern across screens and shows how UI tests validate end-to-end user flows. TaskDetailFragmentTest Walkthrough means add an item, navigate to detail, modify it, and verify the list reflects changes when navigating back.. In practical terms, a guided test: add a task, navigate to detail, edit, save, and verify.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › TaskDetailFragmentTest
Starter Code
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class TaskDetailFragmentTest {

    @get:Rule
    val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(TaskListActivity::class.java)

    @Test
    fun editTaskDetail_updatesAndDisplaysCorrectly() {
        val originalTitle = "Task for Detail"
        val originalDescription = "Original description"
        val updatedDescription = "Updated description for task"

        // Add a new task
        onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_title)).perform(typeText(originalTitle), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.editText_task_description)).perform(typeText(originalDescription), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.button_add_task)).perform(click())

        // Click on the added task to navigate to detail
        onView(withId(R.id.recyclerView_tasks))
            .perform(RecyclerViewActions.actionOnItem< TaskAdapter.TaskViewHolder >(hasDescendant(withText(originalTitle)), click()))

        // Verify detail and edit
        onView(withId(R.id.task_detail_title_edit_text)).check(matches(withText(originalTitle)))
        onView(withId(R.id.task_detail_description_edit_text)).check(matches(withText(originalDescription)))

        onView(withId(R.id.task_detail_description_edit_text))
            .perform(clearText(), typeText(updatedDescription), closeSoftKeyboard())

        onView(withId(R.id.button_save_task)).perform(click())

        // Navigate back and verify updated description in list
        Espresso.pressBack()
        onView(withText(updatedDescription)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))
    }
}
Teaching note

This flow tests adding, navigating, editing, saving, and returning — a full end-to-end UI verification for the task detail scenario.

Checklist
  • Ensure test data is added before interacting with the RecyclerView.
  • Use hasDescendant(withText(...)) to find the item by its title.
  • Close the keyboard after typing and before clicking Save or navigation controls.
Key Takeaway

A well-structured end-to-end UI test verifies that changes made on a detail screen propagate back to the list screen as expected.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Practical fixes for frequent Espresso test failures.

narration.text: This slide walks through common Espresso pitfalls and how to address them. First, the soft keyboard: after typing into an EditText the keyboard can cover buttons, causing clicks to fail. The typical fix is to call closeSoftKeyboard() after typeText. Second, timing issues: even though Espresso synchronizes with many framework events, custom background work may require IdlingResource; avoid Thread. sleep and instead register an appropriate idling resource. Third, incorrect or ambiguous matchers: broad matchers like isDisplayed can match multiple views; prefer withId, withText, or withContentDescription to narrow matches. Fourth, resource IDs: verify you are using the correct R. id values in tests. Fifth, accessibility: use content descriptions or tags for image views and custom views so tests can match them robustly. Sixth, state management: reset app state between tests, for example clearing test data, so tests are independent. Finally, emulator setup: ensure the emulator is responsive and not overloaded, because slow devices can cause timeouts. When a test fails, examine NoMatchingViewException and AmbiguousViewMatcherException to guide corrections. These fixes will help you write more reliable, maintainable UI tests. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Troubleshooting

Common Mistakes

  • Soft keyboard: Omit closeSoftKeyboard and the button may be covered; call closeSoftKeyboard() after typing.
  • Timing issues: Don't use sleep; register an IdlingResource for custom async operations.
  • Ambiguous matchers: Prefer withId or withText instead of broad matchers to avoid multiple matches.
  • Resource IDs: Ensure the R.id used in tests matches the layout under test.
  • Accessibility: Use content descriptions or tags on views so tests find them reliably.
  • State management: Clear persistent state or database entries between tests to keep tests independent.

Debugging tips

Read exceptions

NoMatchingViewException indicates the matcher didn't find a view. AmbiguousViewMatcherException means multiple views matched. Use the stack trace to pinpoint the failing matcher.

Emulator issues

Slow emulators can cause timeouts. Ensure the device has resources and try running tests on a faster emulator or physical device when debugging timing failures.

Pro tip

Prefer explicit controls for test actions (delete button) and test-only hooks to make interactions deterministic.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core terms and patterns from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, UI Testing means instrumented tests that run on device or emulator and validate visible behavior that unit tests cannot exercise. Second, Instrumented Test is the test type that interacts with the Android framework; use androidTestImplementation for dependencies and place tests under src/androidTest. Third, Espresso is the framework for concise and reliable UI tests; it synchronizes with the UI thread and provides onView, matchers, actions, and assertions. Keep these three ideas in mind as you write tests: choose the correct test type, add the proper dependencies, and use Espresso’s find-act-assert pattern to verify user flows. These concepts form the foundation of reliable UI testing on Android. Reflect on which UI flows in your app would benefit most from an Espresso test and which should remain covered by unit tests.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three practical patterns and a takeaway

narration.text: Now focus on three test-building patterns you will use repeatedly. First, ActivityScenarioRule provides a simple way to launch and control an activity under test and should be used to manage the activity lifecycle during instrumented tests. Second, onView is your entry point to locate views — combine it with withId, withText, or withContentDescription to create precise matchers. Third, RecyclerViewActions from espresso-contrib let you interact with list items by position or by matching content; include espresso-contrib in your dependencies when testing RecyclerView. The final takeaway: write tests that are clear about find, act, and assert; avoid brittle sleeps and prefer Espresso synchronization and idling resources when needed. Ask yourself after each test: does it verify user-visible behavior that unit tests cannot? If yes, it belongs in the instrumented suite.
